title: How Does the World Really View China?
gist: Adam Y. Liu argues that despite Pew's July 2026 finding that China now edges out the U.S. in favorability across 25 of 36 countries, this masks a starkly different reality on economic partnership: in 20 of 24 countries surveyed, respondents still prefer economic ties with the U.S., and the gap between favorability and economic preference is driven mainly by perceptions of who is winning the economic race, not genuine affection for either power.

themes.theme: Favorability vs. economic-partnership preference diverge sharply

insights.claim: Pew Research Center found that for the first time in roughly two decades of polling, the world now views China more favorably than the United States, with China rated more favorably than the U.S. in 25 of 36 countries surveyed in July 2026.
insights.speaker: Adam Y. Liu
insights.so_what: A headline data point (25 of 36 countries favor China over the US) that is driving a popular 'US soft power decline' narrative -- but Liu's article exists specifically to challenge the naive reading of this number.
insights.quote: In July, the Pew Research Center found that for the first time in roughly two decades of global polling, the world now views China more favorably than the United States.

insights.claim: Liu's central contrarian finding: despite rising favorability toward China, in 20 of 24 countries surveyed in 2025, more respondents said it was more important for their country to have strong economic ties with the United States than with China.
insights.speaker: Adam Y. Liu
insights.so_what: The single most important data point in the piece: economic-partnership preference (which drives actual national policy) has NOT shifted toward China the way favorability has -- a critical corrective for anyone using favorability polls as a proxy for trade/alliance realignment.
insights.quote: In 2025, the last year for which country-by-country, individual-level data is available, more respondents in 20 out of 24 countries chose economic ties with the United States over ties with China.

insights.claim: In seven countries (Canada, France, Greece, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey), respondents rated China more favorably than the U.S. yet still preferred economic ties with the United States, sometimes by wide margins -- e.g., Sweden preferred U.S. economic ties by 48 percentage points despite favoring China.
insights.speaker: Adam Y. Liu
insights.so_what: A concrete, quotable example (Sweden: pro-China favorability but +48pp preference for U.S. economic ties) demonstrating that favorability polling can badly mislead policy/market expectations about actual economic alignment.
insights.quote: In Sweden, for example, respondents preferred U.S. economic ties to Chinese economic ties by 48 percentage points.

insights.claim: Australia is the sole outlier among surveyed countries: it favors the U.S. on favorability but prefers Chinese economic ties (54% to 43%), a pattern explained by China being Australia's largest export market (30% of all Australian exports) even though half of Australians see China as their top threat.
insights.speaker: Adam Y. Liu
insights.so_what: Illustrates that economic dependency, not sentiment, drives the ties question -- Australia's case is a template for how a country can simultaneously view China as its top threat and top trading partner, relevant to assessing other resource-exporting nations' alignment.
insights.quote: This is not much of a surprise given that China is already the country's largest export destination, accounting for 30 percent of everything Australia sells to the world.

themes.theme: What actually drives the economic-partner choice

insights.claim: Sixty percent of global respondents who preferred economic ties with China did so because they believe China is already the world's leading economic power, compared with only 20 percent of the same group who think the U.S. still leads -- and a mirror pattern holds for U.S.-preferring respondents (58% believe the U.S. leads).
insights.speaker: Adam Y. Liu
insights.so_what: Establishes a clean causal framework: economic-partner preference is driven by perceived economic-hegemon status ('bandwagoning with the perceived winner'), not by favorability/likability -- a reusable model for interpreting future geopolitical opinion polling.
insights.quote: Globally, the individual respondents who preferred China as an economic partner seem to have done so because they believe that China is already the world's leading economic power.

insights.claim: Among those who believe the U.S. still leads the world economy, 75 percent chose economic ties with the U.S. versus 15 percent for China; but among those who believe China has taken the economic lead, only 49 percent chose China while a remarkable 38 percent still chose the U.S. anyway.
insights.speaker: Adam Y. Liu
insights.so_what: Reveals persistent stickiness/loyalty toward the U.S. as an economic partner even among those who believe China now leads economically -- a resilience factor for U.S. soft power that the raw favorability numbers completely obscure.
insights.quote: Yet among those who believe China has taken the lead, 49 percent chose China and a remarkable 38 percent still chose the United States.

insights.claim: China's favorability has risen sharply in several Western countries even as U.S. favorability has fallen to near two-decade lows since Pew began polling in 2002 -- e.g., Italian favorability of China rose from 31% (2022) to 51% (2026), and Spain's rose from 37% (2025) to 54% (2026).
insights.speaker: Adam Y. Liu
insights.so_what: Precise, trackable favorability trendlines (Italy +20pp in 4 years, Spain +17pp in 1 year) that quantify the pace of sentiment shift in traditional U.S. allies -- useful benchmark data for monitoring future Pew releases.
insights.quote: The percentage of Italian respondents with a favorable opinion of China, for instance, increased from 31 percent in 2022 to 51 percent in 2026.

insights.claim: Roughly one in nine respondents across 24 countries surveyed in 2025 preferred maintaining strong economic ties with both the U.S. and China rather than choosing one, with fence-sitting pluralities notably large in Nigeria (39%), Israel (32%), Hungary (27%), Germany (23%), and Turkey (20%).
insights.speaker: Adam Y. Liu
insights.so_what: Identifies a meaningful bloc of hedging countries (led by Nigeria at 39%) that have not committed to either superpower's economic orbit -- a group both Washington and Beijing could still actively court, and one to watch for future alignment shifts.
insights.quote: Thirty-nine percent of Nigerians—a plurality of respondents—declined to choose between Washington and Beijing.

insights.claim: In 20 of 24 countries surveyed, more people named the United States than China as their country's most important ally, and the U.S. won outright majorities in five countries while China led as most important ally in only four (Indonesia, Nigeria, South Africa, and Turkey), with no country giving China a majority.
insights.speaker: Adam Y. Liu
insights.so_what: Quantifies the U.S.'s remaining structural advantage in the alliance dimension (not just economic-partner dimension) of global influence -- a distinct and durable asset the favorability headline obscures entirely.
insights.quote: In 20 of the 24 countries surveyed, more people named the United States than China as their country's most important ally... That gap is Beijing's weakness and Washington's remaining advantage.

insights.claim: Liu warns that the Trump administration's wavering commitment to allies, combined with the incorrect but spreading belief that China has already won the economic race, risks becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy that erodes the U.S.'s remaining economic-partnership advantage.
insights.speaker: Adam Y. Liu
insights.so_what: A explicit risk warning: perception of U.S. decline (even if not yet factually true, since Liu notes the US economy remains the world's largest/most productive) could become self-reinforcing through trade wars and alliance ruptures -- a narrative-risk factor relevant to dollar/reserve-currency and alliance-stability analysis.
insights.quote: Every new trade war and every rupture with an ally risks reinforcing the belief that the U.S. economy is headed in the wrong direction.

insights.claim: Liu's overall thesis is that fears of a wholesale shift in global public opinion toward China are overblown: when forced to choose, most of the world still prefers working with Washington economically, and China should not mistake favorability for actual partnership.
insights.speaker: Adam Y. Liu
insights.so_what: The article's overarching investment-relevant conclusion: don't extrapolate a US-to-China global realignment from favorability polling alone -- trade flows and alliance structures remain stickier and more US-favorable than headline sentiment suggests.
insights.quote: For now, however, fears that public opinion has tilted toward China are overblown. When forced to choose, most of the world still prefers working with Washington.
